A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Debate2Create by the same authors. All pages, equations, tables and figures were readable and inspected, including v2's Appendices A–J; v1 contains no appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original Brax Ant simulation results, including thesis-versus-synthesis performance in Figure 2 and the discovered design's score in Table I.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on five locomotion tasks, component ablations, reward-transfer results and additional analyses in Appendices G–I.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes substantially: v1 generates rewards before synthesis and trains both thesis and synthesis designs; v2 critiques untrained theses, generates rewards after synthesis and trains four synthesized morphologies per round. V2 also restricts pluralistic judging to the round winner instead of each evaluated candidate.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only Ant. V2 retains Ant and adds HalfCheetah, Hopper, Swimmer and Walker2D, substantially broadening the locomotion dynamics and morphologies tested. Both versions use Brax; the MuJoCo terminology does not establish a simulator replacement.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's original-Ant and thesis/synthesis comparisons, v2 evaluates Eureka, RoboMoRe and Bayesian optimization against D2C. Eureka and RoboMoRe were previously cited but not experimentally compared. V2 also adds zero-shot, single-agent and single/no-judge comparison conditions.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a search-then-retraining evaluation design, increases trained candidates from up to eight to sixteen per round and switches the reported backbone from GPT-5 to GPT-5.2. It describes S as cumulative 2D distance from the origin, replacing v1's forward-distance description, and adds normalized reporting and new ablation protocols. These differences prevent direct same-setting score comparisons.

E4.justification: V1 mainly examines thesis/synthesis performance over rounds. V2 adds morphology/reward cross-over experiments, controlled debate and judge ablations, Pareto coverage, reward-code similarity, critique-action associations, a debate transcript, evaluation-metric validation and LLM-backbone sensitivity (Sections 3.2–3.4 and Appendices D, G–I).

E5.justification: V1 reports 95% confidence intervals across reward candidates. V2 reports independent search-seed and final-policy variation, mean±standard deviation and per-seed scores, alongside Welch tests, Hedges' g, FDR correction and association tests. V1 does not disclose a comparable independent-seed count, so this is not evidence of a simple increase in identical repeated runs.

E6.justification: V1 Table I reports Ant scores of 3715.42 for the original robot and 6421.67 for D2C. V2 Table 1 reports 14886±459 and 47084±1469 under its revised setup, not a directly comparable performance gain. Numerous results are added, including reward transfer improving four tasks and the Swimmer exception: D2C morphology with Default reward scores 9379, above full D2C's 8639.

T1.justification: The co-design optimization in Equations (1)–(2) is substantively retained. V2 adds limited mathematical definitions: the cumulative distance-from-origin score and the difference-in-differences interaction term used to characterize co-design synergy. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: V1's Ant-centered claim of 73% improvement expands into claims of outperforming prior methods across five tasks, 18–35% gains over compute-matched zero-shot generation and reward transfer to four default morphologies. Judge-driven Pareto coverage becomes an explicit contribution. The central novelty claim about multi-agent robot co-design is retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations involving transferable reward shaping, super-additive co-design interactions, morphology-dominated Swimmer gains and targeted responses to judge feedback. It qualifies judges' usefulness when stability metrics are uninformative and expands limitations to simulator artifacts, sim-to-real transfer and scaling costs. These substantially extend v1's brief discussion of constrained edits, computation and prompt sensitivity.

D1.justification: Appendices A–F add Ant design prompts, shared control/judge prompts, reward interfaces and expressions, XML parameterization, task-specific RL hyperparameters, baseline implementation details and hardware/time/token/cost accounting. V1 provides only broad implementation descriptions. V2 also promises code and configuration release upon publication; the PDFs do not establish an actual release.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning through quality-diversity research, specification gaming, self-debugging and optimization references. Section 4 and Appendix J articulate distinctions from RoboMoRe, MAP-Elites and other design/reward systems more explicitly than v1, including a new comparison matrix. This exceeds bibliographic or citation-style editing.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, agent responsibilities are reorganized and explained more explicitly, and the experiments become separate setup, main-results, dynamics and ablation subsections. Limitations and conclusion are separated, and a structured appendix with a contents page is introduced. The title and document style also change.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, replaces the original Ant performance display with broader benchmark and multi-panel trajectory plots, and separates morphology illustrations into a cross-method/task grid. New heatmaps, hypervolume plots, statistical tables and transcript illustrations substantially change the visual presentation, alongside a redesigned main-text layout and single-column appendices.

improvement.justification: V2 directly addresses v1's weak support for advantages over single-agent pipelines through controlled component comparisons, evaluated prior methods and independent training repeats. Its prompts and technical appendices substantially improve reproducibility. Important reporting problems remain: Figure 3 does not consistently support the stated 18–35% gaps, Appendix H's run accounting conflicts with the main budget, and the conclusion says 'without retraining' although Table 1 specifies retraining. These weaken precise claims, but the added controls and implementation evidence provide a substantial overall improvement.
